'''Cress''' ('''''Lepidium sativum'''''), sometimes referred to as '''garden cress''' (or curly cress) to distinguish it from [[Cress (disambiguation)|similar plants]] also referred to as cress (from Old English ''cresse''), is a fast-growing, edible [[herb]].

Garden cress is genetically related to [[watercress]] and [[Mustard plant|mustard]], sharing their peppery, tangy flavour and aroma. In some regions, garden cress is known as '''mustard and cress''', '''garden pepper cress''', '''pepperwort''', '''pepper grass''', or '''poor man's pepper'''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cassidy |first=Frederic Gomes |url=http://archive.org/details/dictionaryofamer01arie |title=Dictionary of American regional English |date=1985 |publisher=Cambridge, Mass. : Belknap Press of Harvard University Press |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-674-20511-6 |pages=97}}</ref><ref name="Staub">{{Cite book |last=Staub |first=Jack |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DfxahwLf654C&pg=PA105&dq=%22garden+cress |title=75 Exceptional Herbs for Your Garden |date=2008-08-08 |publisher=Gibbs Smith |isbn=978-1-4236-0877-6 |language=en}}</ref>

This [[annual plant]] can reach a height of {{cvt|60|cm|in|0}}, with many branches on the upper part. The white to pinkish flowers are only {{cvt|2|mm|in|frac=16}} across, clustered in small branched [[raceme]]s.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=z_yezcnaUHQC&pg=PA246&dq=%22garden+cress%22 Vegetables of Canada]. Published by NRC Research Press. {{ISBN|0-660-19503-8}}, {{ISBN|978-0-660-19503-2}}</ref><ref>Boswell, John T. and Sowerby, James.  [https://books.google.com/books?id=-vwnAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA215&dq=%22Lepidium+sativum%22 English Botany: Or, Coloured Figures of British Plants]. Robert Hardwicke, 1863. Page 215.</ref>

When consumed raw, cress is a high-[[nutrient]] food containing substantial content of [[Vitamin A|vitamins A]], [[Vitamin C|C]] and [[Vitamin K|K]] and several [[dietary minerals]].

== In agriculture ==
Cultivation of cress is practical both on mass scales and on the individual scale. Garden cress is suitable for [[hydroponics|hydroponic]] cultivation and thrives in slightly [[alkaline]] water. In many local markets, the demand for hydroponically grown cress can exceed available supply, partially because cress leaves are not suitable for distribution in dried form, so they can only be partially preserved. Consumers commonly acquire cress as [[seed]] or (in Europe) from markets as boxes of young live shoots.<ref name="Canada">[https://books.google.com/books?id=z_yezcnaUHQC&pg=PA246&dq=%22garden+cress%22 Vegetables of Canada]. NRC Research Press. {{ISBN|0-660-19503-8}}, {{ISBN|978-0-660-19503-2}}</ref>

Edible shoots are typically harvested in one to two weeks after planting, when they are {{convert|5|–|13|cm|in|frac=2|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="moosewood">Hirsch, David P.. The [https://archive.org/details/moosewoodrestaur0000hirs/page/74 <!-- quote="garden cress". --> Moosewood Restaurant kitchen garden: creative gardening for the adventurous cook]. Ten Speed Press, 2020. {{ISBN|1-58008-666-7}}, {{ISBN|978-1-58008-666-0}}</ref>

== Culinary uses ==
Garden cress is added to soups, sandwiches and salads for its tangy flavour.<ref name="moosewood"/> It is also eaten as [[sprouting|sprouts]], and the fresh or dried seed pods can be used as a peppery seasoning (''haloon'').<ref name=Canada/> In the [[United Kingdom]], cut cress shoots are commonly used in sandwiches with boiled [[egg (food)|eggs]] and [[mayonnaise]].<ref name="Prestige Egg and Cress sandwich">{{cite web |title=Homegrown Egg & Cress Sandwich |url=https://www.prestige.co.uk/blogs/the-hob-hub/home-grown-egg-cress-sandwich#:~:text=4Spread%20a%20little%20butter,the%20top%20of%20the%20egg. |website=Prestige |publisher=[[Meyer Corporation]] |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref><ref name="Tesco Egg and Cress Sandwich">{{cite web |title=Tesco Egg & Cress Sandwich |url=https://www.tesco.com/groceries/en-GB/products/257328680 |website=Tesco |publisher=[[Tesco]] |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref><ref name="Guardian Perfect Egg Sandwich">{{cite web |last1=Cloake |first1=Felicity |title=How to make the perfect egg mayonnaise sandwich |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2015/sep/16/how-to-make-the-perfect-egg-mayonnaise-sandwich |website=The Guardian |publisher=[[Guardian Media Group]] |access-date=16 November 2023}}</ref>

==Nutrition==

Raw cress is 89% water, 6% [[carbohydrates]] (including 1% [[dietary fiber]]), 3% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]] and less than 1% [[fat]] (table). In a {{convert|100|g|oz|frac=2|abbr=off|adj=on}} reference quantity, raw cress supplies {{convert|134|kJ|kcal|abbr=off}} of [[food energy]] and numerous nutrients in significant content, including [[vitamin K]] (516% of the [[Daily Value]], DV), [[vitamin C]] (83% DV) and [[vitamin A]] (43% DV). Among dietary minerals, [[manganese]] levels are high (26% DV) while several others, including [[potassium]] and [[magnesium]], are in moderate content (table).

== Other uses ==
{{Further|Garden cress oil}}
Garden cress, known as ''chandrashoor'', and the seeds, known as '''aaliv''' or aleev in Marathi, or ''halloon''<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.organicindia.com/PR_OH_chandrashoor.php |title=ORGANIC INDIA, Organic Herbs - Garden Cress |access-date=2010-03-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100206135214/http://organicindia.com/PR_OH_chandrashoor.php |archive-date=2010-02-06 |url-status=dead }}</ref> in India, are commonly used in the system of [[Ayurveda]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Wealth of Indian Raw Materials|year=1979|publisher=Publication and information Directorate|location=New Delhi|pages=CSIR Vol 9, Page 71–72}}</ref> It is also known as ''asario'' in India<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.krishnaindia.in/asario-seeds-suppliers.html|title=Asario Seeds Suppliers|last=mahendra|work=krishna india|access-date=2018-10-11|language=en-gb}}</ref> and the Middle East where it is prized as a medicinal herb, called ''habbat al hamra'' (literally red seeds) in Arabic.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thenationalnews.com/uae/heritage/traditional-cookery-craft-lessons-from-emirati-housewives-1.402345|title=Traditional cookery, craft lessons from Emirati housewives|work=The National|access-date=2018-10-11|language=en}}</ref> In the [[Arabian Peninsula]], the seeds are traditionally mixed with custard to make a hot drink.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://tasteofemarat.wordpress.com/2015/11/01/haba-al-hamra-drink/|title=Haba Al Hamra Drink with Custard|date=2015-11-01|work=Taste of Emarat|access-date=2018-10-11|language=en-US}}</ref>

''L. sativum'' is often used in experiments to teach biology to students in schools. The plant grows readily on damp paper or cotton, and its fast germination and development time make it useful in demonstrating plant growth.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Using Cress in the Lab|url=https://www.saps.org.uk/secondary/teaching-resources/756-using-cress-in-the-lab|access-date=2021-02-27|website=www.saps.org.uk}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-03-25 |title=Garden cress seeds: Benefits, uses and side effects |url=https://www.alwosta.tn/en/blog/75_garden-cress-seeds-benefits-uses-and-side-effects.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921123007/https://www.alwosta.tn/en/blog/75_garden-cress-seeds-benefits-uses-and-side-effects.html |archive-date=2020-09-21 |website=Alwosta}}</ref>
